Renaissance
The Renaissance was a European <color=#3366CC>period of history</color> and cultural movement taking place at the end of the <color=#3366CC>Late Middle</color>
<color=#3366CC>Ages</color> and the beginning of the early modern era. It is variously defined as covering the 15th and 16th centuries or, more
broadly, as lasting from the 14th century to the 17th. It was characterized by the European rediscovery and revival of
the literary, philosophical, and artistic achievements of <color=#3366CC>classical antiquity</color>. Associated with great change in <color=#3366CC>art</color>,

<color=#3366CC>architecture</color>, politics, <color=#3366CC>literature</color>, <color=#3366CC>exploration</color> and <color=#3366CC>technology</color>, the Renaissance was first centered in the <color=#3366CC>Republic of</color>
<color=#3366CC>Florence</color>, then spread to the <color=#3366CC>rest of Italy</color> and later throughout Europe.
The Renaissance's intellectual basis was founded in its version of humanism, derived from the concept of Roman
humanitas and the rediscovery of <color=#3366CC>classical Greek philosophy</color>, such as that of <color=#3366CC>Protagoras</color>, who said that "man is the
measure of all things". Although the invention of <color=#3366CC>metal movable type</color> sped the dissemination of ideas from the later 15th
century, the changes of the Renaissance were not uniform across Europe: the first traces appear in Italy as early as the
late 13th century, in particular with the writings of <color=#3366CC>Dante</color> and the paintings of <color=#3366CC>Giotto</color>.
As a cultural movement, the Renaissance encompassed innovative flowering of literary Latin and an explosion of
vernacular literatures, beginning with the 14th-century resurgence of learning based on classical sources, which
contemporaries credited to <color=#3366CC>Petrarch</color>; the development of linear perspective and other techniques of rendering a more
natural reality in painting; and gradual but widespread <color=#3366CC>educational reform</color>. It saw myriad artistic developments and

contributions from such <color=#3366CC>polymaths</color> as <color=#3366CC>Leonardo da Vinci</color> and <color=#3366CC>Michelangelo</color>, who inspired the term "<color=#3366CC>Renaissance man</color>".
In politics, the Renaissance contributed to the development of the customs and conventions of diplomacy. The period
also saw revolutions in <color=#3366CC>printing</color> and <color=#3366CC>navigation</color>, as well as the <color=#3366CC>introduction of modern banking</color> and the field of
<color=#3366CC>accounting</color>.
Period
The Renaissance <color=#3366CC>began in Italy</color> during the <color=#3366CC>crisis of the Late Middle Ages</color>. It had a different period and characteristics
north of the Alps and in Spain. In Italy, the period conventionally ends with the waning of humanism, and the advent of
the <color=#3366CC>Reformation</color> (1517), the Sack of Rome (1527) or the <color=#3366CC>Counter-Reformation</color> (1545), and in art, the <color=#3366CC>Baroque</color> period.
Proponents of a "long Renaissance," however, may propose that (outside of Italy) the period extended into the 17th
century.
The traditional view focuses more on the Renaissance's early modern aspects and argues that it was a break from the
past, but many historians today focus more on its medieval aspects and argue that it was an extension of the Middle
Ages.
Italian Renaissance
The beginnings of the period—the early Renaissance of the 15th century and the Italian Proto-Renaissance from
around 1250 or 1300—overlap considerably with the <color=#3366CC>Late Middle Ages</color>, conventionally dated to c. 1350–1500, and the
Middle Ages themselves were a long period filled with gradual changes, like the modern age; as a transitional period
between both, the Renaissance has close similarities to both, especially the late and early sub-periods of either.
The Renaissance began in <color=#3366CC>Florence</color>, one of the many states of Italy. The Italian Renaissance concluded in 1527 when
<color=#3366CC>Holy Roman Emperor Charles V</color> launched an assault on Rome during the war of the League of Cognac. Nevertheless,
its impact endured in the art of renowned Italian painters like <color=#3366CC>Tintoretto</color>, <color=#3366CC>Sofonisba Anguissola</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Paolo Veronese</color>,
who continued their work during the mid-to-late 16th century.
Various theories have been proposed to account for its origins and characteristics, focusing on a variety of factors,
including Florence's social and civic peculiarities at the time: its political structure, the patronage of its dominant family,
the <color=#3366CC>Medici</color>, and the migration of Greek scholars and their texts to Italy following the <color=#3366CC>fall of Constantinople</color> to the

<color=#3366CC>Ottoman Empire</color>. Other major centers were <color=#3366CC>Venice</color>, <color=#3366CC>Genoa</color>, <color=#3366CC>Milan</color>, <color=#3366CC>Rome</color> during the Renaissance Papacy, and <color=#3366CC>Naples</color>.
From Italy, the Renaissance spread throughout Europe and also to American, African and Asian territories ruled by the
European colonial powers of the time or where Christian missionaries were active.
The Renaissance has a long and complex <color=#3366CC>historiography</color>, and in line with general skepticism of discrete periodizations,
there has been much debate among historians reacting to the 19th-century glorification of the "Renaissance" and
individual cultural heroes as "Renaissance men", questioning the usefulness of Renaissance as a term and as a
historical delineation.
Some observers have questioned whether the Renaissance was a cultural "advance" from the Middle Ages, instead
seeing it as a period of pessimism and <color=#3366CC>nostalgia</color> for <color=#3366CC>classical antiquity</color>, while social and economic historians, especially
of the longue durée, have instead focused on the continuity between the two eras, which are linked, as <color=#3366CC>Panofsky</color>
observed, "by a thousand ties".
Overview
The Renaissance was a cultural movement that profoundly affected European intellectual life in the early modern
period. Beginning in Italy, and spreading to the rest of Europe by the 16th century, its influence was felt in <color=#3366CC>art</color>,

<color=#3366CC>architecture</color>, <color=#3366CC>philosophy</color>, <color=#3366CC>literature</color>, <color=#3366CC>music</color>, science, <color=#3366CC>technology</color>, politics, religion, and other aspects of intellectual
inquiry. Renaissance scholars employed the humanist method in study, and searched for realism and human emotion
in art.
Renaissance humanists such as Poggio Bracciolini sought out in Europe's monastic libraries the Latin literary,
historical, and oratorical texts of <color=#3366CC>antiquity</color>, while the <color=#3366CC>fall of Constantinople</color> (1453) generated a wave of émigré Greek
scholars bringing precious manuscripts in <color=#3366CC>ancient Greek</color>, many of which had fallen into obscurity in the West. It was in
their new focus on literary and historical texts that Renaissance scholars differed so markedly from the medieval
scholars of the <color=#3366CC>Renaissance of the 12th century</color>, who had focused on studying <color=#3366CC>Greek</color> and <color=#3366CC>Arabic</color> works of natural
sciences, philosophy, and mathematics, rather than on such cultural texts.
In the revival of <color=#3366CC>neoplatonism</color>, Renaissance humanists did not reject <color=#3366CC>Christianity</color>; on the contrary, many of the
Renaissance's greatest works were devoted to it, and the Church patronized many works of Renaissance art. But a
subtle shift took place in the way that intellectuals approached religion that was reflected in many other areas of cultural
life. In addition, many Greek Christian works, including the Greek New Testament, were brought back from <color=#3366CC>Byzantium</color>
to Western Europe and engaged Western scholars for the first time since late antiquity. This new engagement with
Greek Christian works, and particularly the return to the original Greek of the New Testament promoted by humanists
Lorenzo Valla and <color=#3366CC>Erasmus</color>, helped pave the way for the <color=#3366CC>Reformation</color>.
Well after the first artistic return to <color=#3366CC>classicism</color> had been exemplified in the sculpture of <color=#3366CC>Nicola Pisano</color>, Florentine
painters led by <color=#3366CC>Masaccio</color> strove to portray the human form realistically, developing techniques to render <color=#3366CC>perspective</color>
and light more naturally. <color=#3366CC>Political philosophers</color>, most famously <color=#3366CC>Niccolò Machiavelli</color>, sought to describe political life as it
really was, that is, to understand it rationally. A critical contribution to Italian Renaissance humanism, Giovanni Pico
della Mirandola wrote De hominis dignitate (Oration on the Dignity of Man, 1486), a series of theses on philosophy,
natural thought, faith, and magic defended against any opponent on the grounds of reason. In addition to studying
classical Latin and Greek, Renaissance authors also began increasingly to use vernacular languages; combined with
the introduction of the <color=#3366CC>printing press</color>, this allowed many more people access to books, especially the Bible.
In all, the Renaissance can be viewed as an attempt by intellectuals to study and improve the secular and worldly, both
through the revival of ideas from antiquity and through novel approaches to thought. Political philosopher Hans Kohn
describes it as an age where "Men looked for new foundations"; some like <color=#3366CC>Erasmus</color> and <color=#3366CC>Thomas More</color> envisioned new
reformed spiritual foundations, others, in the words of <color=#3366CC>Machiavelli</color>, una lunga sperienza delle cose moderne ed una
continua lezione delle antiche (a long experience with modern life and a continuous learning from antiquity).
Sociologist Rodney Stark plays down the Renaissance in favor of the earlier innovations of the Italian city-states in the
<color=#3366CC>High Middle Ages</color>, which married responsive government, Christianity and the birth of <color=#3366CC>capitalism</color>. This analysis argues
that, whereas the great European states (France and Spain) were <color=#3366CC>absolute monarchies</color>, and others were under direct
Church control, the independent <color=#3366CC>city-republics</color> of Italy took over the principles of capitalism invented on monastic
estates and set off a vast unprecedented Commercial Revolution that preceded and financed the Renaissance.
Historian Leon Poliakov offers a critical view in his seminal study of European racist thought: The Aryan Myth.
According to Poliakov, the use of ethnic origin myths are first used by Renaissance humanists "in the service of a new
born chauvinism".
Origins
Many argue that the ideas characterizing the Renaissance had their origin in <color=#3366CC>Florence</color> at the turn of the 13th and 14th
centuries, in particular with the writings of <color=#3366CC>Dante Alighieri</color> (1265–1321) and <color=#3366CC>Petrarch</color> (1304–1374), as well as the
paintings of <color=#3366CC>Giotto di Bondone</color> (1267–1337). Some writers date the Renaissance quite precisely; one proposed starting
point is 1401, when the rival geniuses <color=#3366CC>Lorenzo Ghiberti</color> and <color=#3366CC>Filippo Brunelleschi</color> competed for the contract to build the
bronze doors for the Baptistery of the <color=#3366CC>Florence Cathedral</color> (Ghiberti won). Others see more general competition
between artists and polymaths such as Brunelleschi, Ghiberti, <color=#3366CC>Donatello</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Masaccio</color> for artistic commissions as
sparking the creativity of the Renaissance.
Yet it remains much debated why the Renaissance began in Italy, and why it began when it did. Accordingly, several
theories have been put forward to explain its origins. Peter Rietbergen posits that various influential Proto-Renaissance
movements started from roughly 1300 onwards across many regions of <color=#3366CC>Europe</color>.
Latin and Greek phases of Renaissance humanism
In stark contrast to the <color=#3366CC>High Middle Ages</color>, when Latin scholars focused almost entirely on studying Greek and Arabic
works of natural science, philosophy and mathematics, Renaissance scholars were most interested in recovering and
studying Latin and Greek literary, historical, and oratorical texts. Broadly speaking, this began in the 14th century with a
Latin phase, when Renaissance scholars such as <color=#3366CC>Petrarch</color>, Coluccio Salutati (1331–1406), Niccolò de' Niccoli
(1364–1437), and Poggio Bracciolini (1380–1459) scoured the libraries of Europe in search of works by such Latin

authors as <color=#3366CC>Cicero</color>, <color=#3366CC>Lucretius</color>, <color=#3366CC>Livy</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Seneca</color>. By the early 15th century, the bulk of the surviving such Latin literature
had been recovered; the Greek phase of Renaissance humanism was under way, as Western European scholars
turned to recovering ancient Greek literary, historical, oratorical and theological texts.
Unlike with Latin texts, which had been preserved and studied in Western Europe since late antiquity, the study of
ancient Greek texts was very limited in medieval Western Europe. Ancient Greek works on science, mathematics, and
philosophy had been studied since the <color=#3366CC>High Middle Ages</color> in Western Europe and in the <color=#3366CC>Islamic Golden Age</color> (normally in
translation), but Greek literary, oratorical and historical works (such as <color=#3366CC>Homer</color>, the Greek dramatists, <color=#3366CC>Demosthenes</color> and
<color=#3366CC>Thucydides</color>) were not studied in either the Latin or medieval <color=#3366CC>Islamic worlds</color>; in the Middle Ages these sorts of texts
were only studied by Byzantine scholars. Some argue that the Timurid Renaissance in <color=#3366CC>Samarkand</color> and <color=#3366CC>Herat</color>, whose
magnificence toned with Florence as the center of a cultural rebirth, were linked to the <color=#3366CC>Ottoman Empire</color>, whose
conquests led to the migration of Greek scholars to Italian cities. One of the greatest achievements of Renaissance
scholars was to bring this entire class of Greek cultural works back into Western Europe for the first time since late
antiquity.
<color=#3366CC>Muslim</color> logicians, most notably <color=#3366CC>Avicenna</color> and <color=#3366CC>Averroes</color>, had inherited Greek ideas after they had invaded and
conquered <color=#3366CC>Egypt</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Levant</color>. Their translations and commentaries on these ideas worked their way through the
Arab West into <color=#3366CC>Iberia</color> and <color=#3366CC>Sicily</color>, which became important centers for this transmission of ideas. Between the 11th and
13th centuries, many schools dedicated to the translation of philosophical and scientific works from <color=#3366CC>Classical Arabic</color> to
<color=#3366CC>Medieval Latin</color> were established in Iberia, most notably the Toledo School of Translators. This work of translation from
Islamic culture, though largely unplanned and disorganized, constituted one of the greatest transmissions of ideas in
history.
The movement to reintegrate the regular study of Greek literary, historical, oratorical, and theological texts back into the
Western European curriculum is usually dated to the 1396 invitation from Coluccio Salutati to the Byzantine diplomat
and scholar Manuel Chrysoloras (c. 1355–1415) to teach Greek in Florence. This legacy was continued by a number of
expatriate Greek scholars, from Basilios Bessarion to Leo Allatius.
Social and political structures in Italy
The unique political structures of <color=#3366CC>Italy</color> during the <color=#3366CC>Late Middle Ages</color> have led some to theorize that its unusual social
climate allowed the emergence of a rare cultural efflorescence. Italy did not exist as a <color=#3366CC>political entity</color> in the early modern
period. Instead, it was divided into smaller city-states and territories: the <color=#3366CC>Neapolitans</color> controlled the south, the

<color=#3366CC>Florentines</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Romans</color> at the center, the <color=#3366CC>Milanese</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Genoese</color> to the north and west respectively, and the
<color=#3366CC>Venetians</color> to the north east. 15th-century Italy was one of the most <color=#3366CC>urbanized</color> areas in Europe. Many of its cities stood
among the ruins of ancient Roman buildings; it seems likely that the classical nature of the Renaissance was linked to
its origin in the Roman Empire's heartland.
Historian and political philosopher <color=#3366CC>Quentin Skinner</color> points out that Otto of Freising (c. 1114–1158), a German bishop
visiting north Italy during the 12th century, noticed a widespread new form of political and social organization, observing
that Italy appeared to have exited from <color=#3366CC>feudalism</color> so that its society was based on merchants and commerce. Linked to
this was anti-monarchical thinking, represented in the famous early Renaissance <color=#3366CC>fresco</color> cycle The Allegory of Good
and Bad Government by <color=#3366CC>Ambrogio Lorenzetti</color> (painted 1338–1340), whose strong message is about the virtues of
fairness, justice, republicanism and good administration. Holding both Church and <color=#3366CC>Empire</color> at bay, these city republics
were devoted to notions of liberty. Skinner reports that there were many defences of liberty such as the Matteo Palmieri
(1406–1475) celebration of Florentine genius not only in art, sculpture and architecture, but "the remarkable
efflorescence of moral, social and political philosophy that occurred in Florence at the same time".
Even cities and states beyond central Italy, such as the Republic of Florence at this time, were also notable for their
<color=#3366CC>merchant republics</color>, especially the Republic of Venice. Although in practice these were <color=#3366CC>oligarchical</color>, and bore little
resemblance to a modern <color=#3366CC>democracy</color>, they did have democratic features and were responsive states, with forms of
participation in governance and belief in liberty. The relative political freedom they afforded was conducive to academic
and artistic advancement. Likewise, the position of Italian cities such as Venice as great trading centres made them
intellectual crossroads. <color=#3366CC>Merchants</color> brought with them ideas from far corners of the globe, particularly the <color=#3366CC>Levant</color>. Venice
was Europe's gateway to trade with the East, and a producer of fine glass, while Florence was a capital of textiles. The
wealth such business brought to Italy meant large public and private artistic projects could be commissioned and
individuals had more leisure time for study.
Black Death
One theory that has been advanced is that the devastation in <color=#3366CC>Florence</color> caused by the <color=#3366CC>Black Death</color>, which hit Europe
between 1348 and 1350, resulted in a shift in the world view of people in 14th century Italy. Italy was particularly badly
hit by the plague, and it has been speculated that the resulting familiarity with death caused thinkers to dwell more on
their lives on Earth, rather than on <color=#3366CC>spirituality</color> and the <color=#3366CC>afterlife</color>. It has also been argued that the Black Death prompted a
new wave of piety, manifested in the <color=#3366CC>sponsorship</color> of religious works of art. However, this does not fully explain why the
Renaissance occurred specifically in Italy in the 14th century. The Black Death was a <color=#3366CC>pandemic</color> that affected all of
Europe in the ways described, not only Italy. The Renaissance's emergence in Italy was most likely the result of the
complex interaction of the above factors.
The plague was carried by fleas on sailing vessels returning from the ports of Asia, spreading quickly due to lack of
proper sanitation: the population of <color=#3366CC>England</color>, then about 4.2 million, lost 1.4 million people to the <color=#3366CC>bubonic plague</color>.
Florence's population was nearly halved in the year 1348. As a result of the decimation in the populace the value of the
working class increased, and commoners came to enjoy more freedom. To answer the increased need for labor,
workers traveled in search of the most favorable position economically.
The demographic decline due to the plague had economic consequences: the prices of food dropped and land values
declined by 30–40% in most parts of Europe between 1350 and 1400. Landholders faced a great loss, but for ordinary
men and women it was a windfall. The survivors of the plague found not only that the prices of food were cheaper but
also that lands were more abundant, and many of them inherited property from their dead relatives.
The spread of disease was significantly more rampant in areas of poverty. <color=#3366CC>Epidemics</color> ravaged cities, particularly
children. Plagues were easily spread by lice, unsanitary drinking water, armies, or by poor sanitation. Children were hit
the hardest because many diseases, such as <color=#3366CC>typhus</color> and congenital syphilis, target the immune system, leaving young
children without a fighting chance. Children in city dwellings were more affected by the spread of disease than the
children of the wealthy.
The Black Death caused greater upheaval to Florence's social and political structure than later epidemics. Despite a
significant number of deaths among members of the ruling classes, the government of Florence continued to function
during this period. Formal meetings of elected representatives were suspended during the height of the epidemic due
to the chaotic conditions in the city, but a small group of officials was appointed to conduct the affairs of the city, which
ensured continuity of government.
Cultural conditions in Florence
It has long been a matter of debate why the Renaissance began in <color=#3366CC>Florence</color>, and not elsewhere in Italy. Scholars have
noted several features unique to Florentine cultural life that may have caused such a cultural movement. Many have
emphasized the role played by the <color=#3366CC>Medici</color>, a banking family and later <color=#3366CC>ducal ruling house</color>, in patronizing and stimulating
the arts. Some historians have postulated that Florence was the birthplace of the Renaissance as a result of luck, i.e.,
because "<color=#3366CC>Great Men</color>" were born there by chance: Leonardo, Botticelli and Michelangelo were all born in <color=#3366CC>Tuscany</color>.
Arguing that such chance seems improbable, other historians have contended that these "Great Men" were only able to
rise to prominence because of the prevailing cultural conditions at the time.
<color=#3366CC>Lorenzo de' Medici</color> (1449–1492) was the catalyst for an enormous amount of arts patronage, encouraging his
countrymen to commission works from the leading artists of Florence, including <color=#3366CC>Leonardo da Vinci</color>, <color=#3366CC>Sandro Botticelli</color>,
and <color=#3366CC>Michelangelo Buonarroti</color>. Works by Neri di Bicci, Botticelli, Leonardo, and Filippino Lippi had been commissioned
additionally by the Convent of San Donato in Scopeto in Florence.
The Renaissance was certainly underway before Lorenzo de' Medici came to power – indeed, before the Medici family
itself achieved hegemony in Florentine society.
Characteristics
Humanism
In some ways, Renaissance humanism was not a philosophy but a method of learning. In contrast to the medieval
<color=#3366CC>scholastic</color> mode, which focused on resolving contradictions between authors, Renaissance humanists would study
ancient texts in their original languages and appraise them through a combination of reasoning and empirical evidence.
Humanist education was based on the programme of Studia Humanitatis, the study of five humanities: <color=#3366CC>poetry</color>,

<color=#3366CC>grammar</color>, <color=#3366CC>history</color>, <color=#3366CC>moral philosophy</color>, and <color=#3366CC>rhetoric</color>. Although historians have sometimes struggled to define humanism
precisely, most have settled on "a middle of the road definition... the movement to recover, interpret, and assimilate the
language, literature, learning and values of ancient Greece and Rome". Above all, humanists asserted "the genius of
man ... the unique and extraordinary ability of the human mind".
Humanist scholars shaped the intellectual landscape throughout the early modern period. Political philosophers such
as Niccolò Machiavelli and <color=#3366CC>Thomas More</color> revived the ideas of Greek and Roman thinkers and applied them in critiques
of contemporary government, following the Islamic steps of <color=#3366CC>Ibn Khaldun</color>. Pico della Mirandola wrote the "manifesto" of
the Renaissance, the Oration on the Dignity of Man, a vibrant defence of thinking. Matteo Palmieri (1406–1475),
another humanist, is most known for his work Della vita civile ("On Civic Life"; printed 1528), which advocated civic
humanism, and for his influence in refining the Tuscan vernacular to the same level as Latin. Palmieri drew on Roman
philosophers and theorists, especially <color=#3366CC>Cicero</color>, who, like Palmieri, lived an active public life as a citizen and official, as
well as a theorist and philosopher and also Quintilian. Perhaps the most succinct expression of his perspective on
humanism is in a 1465 poetic work La città di vita, but an earlier work, Della vita civile, is more wide-ranging.
Composed as a series of dialogues set in a country house in the Mugello countryside outside Florence during the
plague of 1430, Palmieri expounds on the qualities of the ideal citizen. The dialogues include ideas about how children
develop mentally and physically, how citizens can conduct themselves morally, how citizens and states can ensure
probity in public life, and an important debate on the difference between that which is pragmatically useful and that
which is honest.
The humanists believed that it is important to transcend to the afterlife with a perfect mind and body, which could be
attained with education. The purpose of humanism was to create a universal man whose person combined intellectual
and physical excellence and who was capable of functioning honorably in virtually any situation. This ideology was
referred to as the <color=#3366CC>uomo universale</color>, an ancient Greco-Roman ideal. Education during the Renaissance was mainly
composed of ancient literature and history as it was thought that the classics provided moral instruction and an
intensive understanding of human behavior.
Humanism and libraries
A unique characteristic of some Renaissance libraries is that they were open to the public. These libraries were places
where ideas were exchanged and where scholarship and reading were considered both pleasurable and beneficial to
the mind and soul. As freethinking was a hallmark of the age, many libraries contained a wide range of writers.
Classical texts could be found alongside humanist writings. These informal associations of intellectuals profoundly
influenced Renaissance culture. An essential tool of Renaissance librarianship was the catalog that listed, described,
and classified a library's books. Some of the richest "bibliophiles" built libraries as temples to books and knowledge. A
number of libraries appeared as manifestations of immense wealth joined with a love of books. In some cases,
cultivated library builders were also committed to offering others the opportunity to use their collections. Prominent
aristocrats and princes of the Church created great libraries for the use of their courts, called "court libraries", and were
housed in lavishly designed monumental buildings decorated with ornate woodwork, and the walls adorned with
frescoes (Murray, Stuart A.P.).
Art
Renaissance art marks a cultural rebirth at the close of the Middle Ages and rise of the Modern world. One of the
distinguishing features of Renaissance art was its development of highly realistic linear perspective. <color=#3366CC>Giotto di Bondone</color>
(1267–1337) is credited with first treating a painting as a window into space, but it was not until the demonstrations of
architect <color=#3366CC>Filippo Brunelleschi</color> (1377–1446) and the subsequent writings of <color=#3366CC>Leon Battista Alberti</color> (1404–1472) that
perspective was formalized as an artistic technique.
The development of <color=#3366CC>perspective</color> was part of a wider trend toward <color=#3366CC>realism</color> in the arts. Painters developed other
techniques, studying light, shadow, and, famously in the case of <color=#3366CC>Leonardo da Vinci</color>, <color=#3366CC>human anatomy</color>. Underlying these
changes in artistic method was a renewed desire to depict the beauty of nature and to unravel the axioms of <color=#3366CC>aesthetics</color>,
with the works of Leonardo, <color=#3366CC>Michelangelo</color> and <color=#3366CC>Raphael</color> representing artistic pinnacles that were much imitated by other
artists. Other notable artists include <color=#3366CC>Sandro Botticelli</color>, working for the Medici in Florence, <color=#3366CC>Donatello</color>, another Florentine,
and <color=#3366CC>Titian</color> in Venice, among others.
In the <color=#3366CC>Low Countries</color>, a particularly vibrant artistic culture developed. The work of Hugo van der Goes and <color=#3366CC>Jan van</color>
<color=#3366CC>Eyck</color> was particularly influential on the development of painting in Italy, both technically with the introduction of <color=#3366CC>oil paint</color>
and canvas, and stylistically in terms of naturalism in representation. Later, the work of <color=#3366CC>Pieter Brueghel the Elder</color> would
inspire artists to depict themes of everyday life.
In architecture, Filippo Brunelleschi was foremost in studying the remains of ancient classical buildings. With
rediscovered knowledge from the 1st-century writer <color=#3366CC>Vitruvius</color> and the flourishing discipline of mathematics, Brunelleschi
formulated the Renaissance style that emulated and improved on classical forms. His major feat of engineering was
building the dome of <color=#3366CC>Florence Cathedral</color>. Another building demonstrating this style is the Basilica of Sant'Andrea,
Mantua, built by Alberti. The outstanding architectural work of the High Renaissance was the rebuilding of <color=#3366CC>St. Peter's</color>
<color=#3366CC>Basilica</color>, combining the skills of <color=#3366CC>Bramante</color>, Michelangelo, Raphael, Sangallo and <color=#3366CC>Maderno</color>.
During the Renaissance, architects aimed to use columns, pilasters, and entablatures as an integrated system. The
Roman orders types of columns are used: Tuscan and Composite. These can either be structural, supporting an
arcade or architrave, or purely decorative, set against a wall in the form of pilasters. One of the first buildings to use
pilasters as an integrated system was in the Old Sacristy (1421–1440) by Brunelleschi. Arches, semi-circular or (in the
<color=#3366CC>Mannerist</color> style) segmental, are often used in arcades, supported on piers or columns with capitals. There may be a
section of entablature between the capital and the springing of the arch. Alberti was one of the first to use the arch on a
monumental. Renaissance vaults do not have ribs; they are semi-circular or segmental and on a square plan, unlike the
<color=#3366CC>Gothic</color> vault, which is frequently rectangular.
Renaissance artists were not pagans, although they admired antiquity and kept some ideas and symbols of the
medieval past. <color=#3366CC>Nicola Pisano</color> (c. 1220 – c. 1278) imitated classical forms by portraying scenes from the Bible. His
Annunciation, from the Pisa Baptistry, demonstrates that classical models influenced Italian art before the Renaissance
took root as a literary movement.
Printing

From a single print shop in <color=#3366CC>Mainz</color>, Germany around 1440, the <color=#3366CC>movable type</color> <color=#3366CC>printing-press</color> had <color=#3366CC>spread to no less than</color>
<color=#3366CC>around 270 cities</color> in Central, Western and Eastern Europe and had already produced more than 20 million volumes by
the end of the 15th century. Printing made scholarly books more widely accessible, allowing researchers to consult
ancient texts freely and to compare their own observations with those of fellow scholars. Printing ended the manuscript
culture of the Middle Ages, where <color=#3366CC>facts</color> were few and far between, and replaced it with a printing culture where reliable
and documented facts rapidly proliferated and became the secure foundation for scientific knowledge.
Navigation and geography
In 1492, <color=#3366CC>Christopher Columbus</color> sailed across the Atlantic Ocean from Spain seeking a direct route to India of the <color=#3366CC>Delhi</color>
<color=#3366CC>Sultanate</color>. He accidentally stumbled upon the Americas, but believed he had reached the East Indies. The Portuguese
explorer <color=#3366CC>Vasco da Gama</color> completed the first recorded trip directly from Europe to the Indian subcontinent (1497-1499).
The Florentine <color=#3366CC>Amerigo Vespucci</color>'s <color=#3366CC>Mundus Novus</color> letter, published in 1503 and repeatedly reprinted, provided the first
explicit articulation in print that the lands encountered by European navigators to the West were not the edges of Asia,
but rather an <color=#3366CC>entirely different continent</color> (a "New World").Between 1519 and 1522, the <color=#3366CC>Magellan–Elcano expedition</color>
achieved the first circumnavigation of Earth in history, including the first crossing of the Pacific by a European
expedition, revealing the vast scale of that ocean. Every continent was visited and mostly mapped by Europeans,
except the south polar continent now known as <color=#3366CC>Antarctica</color>.
The discovery of continents that were completely unknown to the <color=#3366CC>ancients</color> had a profound impact on European
intellectual life in the 16th century. By revealing a "New World" unknown to the ancients, the European encounter with
the <color=#3366CC>Americas</color> also specifically undermined the authority of <color=#3366CC>Claudius Ptolemy</color>, the 2nd-century scholar whose
<color=#3366CC>geographic</color> and <color=#3366CC>astronomical</color> models had long been considered infallible.
Religion
The new ideals of humanism, although more secular in some aspects, developed against a Christian backdrop,
especially in the Northern Renaissance. Much, if not most, of the new art was commissioned by or in dedication to the
<color=#3366CC>Roman Catholic Church</color>. However, the Renaissance had a profound effect on contemporary <color=#3366CC>theology</color>, particularly in the
way people perceived the relationship between man and God. Many of the period's foremost theologians were

followers of the humanist method, including <color=#3366CC>Erasmus</color>, <color=#3366CC>Huldrych Zwingli</color>, <color=#3366CC>Thomas More</color>, <color=#3366CC>Martin Luther</color>, and <color=#3366CC>John Calvin</color>.
The Renaissance began in times of religious turmoil. The Late Middle Ages was a period of political intrigue
surrounding the <color=#3366CC>Papacy</color>, culminating in the <color=#3366CC>Western Schism</color>, in which three men simultaneously claimed to be true
<color=#3366CC>Bishop</color> of Rome. While the schism was resolved by the Council of Constance (1414), a resulting reform movement
known as Conciliarism sought to limit the power of the pope. Although the papacy eventually emerged supreme in
ecclesiastical matters by the Fifth Council of the Lateran (1511), it was dogged by continued accusations of corruption,
most famously in the person of <color=#3366CC>Pope Alexander VI</color>, who was accused variously of simony, <color=#3366CC>nepotism</color>, and fathering
children (most of whom were married off, presumably for the consolidation of power) while a cardinal.
Churchmen such as Erasmus and Luther proposed reform to the Church, often based on humanist textual criticism of
the <color=#3366CC>New Testament</color>. In October 1517, Luther published the <color=#3366CC>Ninety-five Theses</color>, challenging papal authority and
criticizing its perceived corruption, particularly with regard to instances of sold <color=#3366CC>indulgences</color>. The 95 Theses led to the
<color=#3366CC>Reformation</color>, a break with the Roman Catholic Church that previously claimed hegemony in <color=#3366CC>Western Europe</color>.
Humanism and the Renaissance therefore played a direct role in sparking the Reformation, as well as in many other
contemporaneous religious debates and conflicts.
Pope Paul III came to the papal throne (1534–1549) after the sack of Rome in 1527, with uncertainties prevalent in the
Catholic Church following the Reformation. Nicolaus Copernicus dedicated <color=#3366CC>De revolutionibus orbium coelestium</color> (On
the Revolutions of the Celestial Spheres) to Paul III, who became the grandfather of Alessandro Farnese, who had
paintings by <color=#3366CC>Titian</color>, <color=#3366CC>Michelangelo</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Raphael</color>, as well as an important collection of drawings, and who commissioned
the masterpiece of Giulio Clovio, arguably the last major <color=#3366CC>illuminated manuscript</color>, the Farnese Hours.
Natural philosophy
In the first period of the <color=#3366CC>Italian Renaissance</color>, humanists favored the study of <color=#3366CC>humanities</color> over <color=#3366CC>natural philosophy</color> or
<color=#3366CC>applied mathematics</color>, and their reverence for classical sources further enshrined the <color=#3366CC>Aristotelian</color> and <color=#3366CC>Ptolemaic</color> views
of the universe. Writing around 1450, <color=#3366CC>Nicholas of Cusa</color> claimed that the universe must be infinite in extent and
therefore devoid of a center.
Natural philosophy and art were intermingled in the early Renaissance, with polymath artists such as <color=#3366CC>Leonardo da Vinci</color>
making observational drawings of anatomy and nature. Leonardo set up controlled experiments in water flow, medical
dissection, and systematic study of movement and aerodynamics, and he devised principles of research method that
led Fritjof Capra to classify him as the "father of modern science". Other examples of Da Vinci's contribution during this
period include machines designed to saw marbles and lift monoliths, and new discoveries in acoustics, botany,
geology, anatomy, and mechanics.
As the Reformation and <color=#3366CC>Counter-Reformation</color> clashed, the Northern Renaissance showed a decisive shift in focus from
Aristotelian natural philosophy to chemistry and the biological sciences (botany, anatomy, and medicine).
<color=#3366CC>Nikolas Copernicus</color>, in <color=#3366CC>De revolutionibus orbium coelestium</color> (On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres), posited that
the Earth moved around the Sun.
Applied innovation extended to commerce. At the end of the 15th century, <color=#3366CC>Luca Pacioli</color> published the first work on
<color=#3366CC>bookkeeping</color>, making him the founder of <color=#3366CC>accounting</color>.
Medicine
References to Greek Antiquity appeared in medical texts and theories specifically to Aristotle, Plato, and skepticism.
The most prominent classical focus in medicine was to <color=#3366CC>Hippocrates (460-370 BCE)</color> and <color=#3366CC>Galen (129-216)</color>. Realist art
blended with anatomical advancements in medicine. Medical scholars enlisted artists to create new works. <color=#3366CC>Andreas</color>
<color=#3366CC>Vesalius (1514-64)</color>, a Flemish physician, published the De humani corporis fabrica libri septem in 1543. It was an
anatomical encyclopedia renowned for its accurate drawings of the human anatomy. It became the basis for
Renaissance anatomy as it was the most detailed account of the human body written. Another writer of anatomy was
Jacopo Berengario da Carpi (d. 1530), a professor at Bologna, who wrote The Commentary in 1521, complete with
anatomical illustrations. The intense focus on classic theory was not without pushback, most notably from Vesalius in
his critiques of Galen in various texts. Despite this new scholarship, the heart of these works was still Galen's humoral
theory and therapeutics, which would continue for many centuries.
The focus on anatomy was partly a continued response to humanism, while simultaneously highlighting observation
and description. Dissections became more frequent and prestigious, while autopsies gained relevance in medical
education. New surgical techniques developed, and there was a new interest in alchemical/chymiatric methods as a
result of the focus on empirical knowledge. New movements sprang up, completely devoted to the study of chemical
and alchemical medicine. The Paracelsian movement was inspired by the chemical physician <color=#3366CC>Paracelsus (1493-1541)</color>,
and it emphasized producing transformative and life-prolonging remedies. This movement rejected Galenic humoral
theory in favor of a chemical understanding of medicine. The Paracelsian movement was controversial, especially to
universities and scholastic physicians.
Written works and texts remained central to the medical field. The invention of the printing press in 1457 allowed for
medical treatises to be reproduced more quickly and in vernacular languages, which widened the literate field beyond
elites and religious figures. Johannes Oporinus was one of the most famous Renaissance publishers of medicine. The
printing press aided the growing focus on natural medicine by publishing textbooks on plants and botany. Leonhart
Fuchs, a German herbalist, published his treatise on medical botany, "De Historia Stirpium," in 1542. In 1544, Pietro
Andrea Mattioli published his commentary on Dioscorides, an ancient Greek physician and botanist. Fuchs was the first
herbalist to describe American plant introductions like maize.
The Spanish and Portuguese exploration of the Americas opened up new herbs and remedies to Renaissance
Medicine, as well as diseases. The wood from the Guaiac tree was imported as early as 1508 from the Caribbean to be
used against the new world disease sweeping Europe. The disease was syphilis, and as reported by the humanist
Ulrich von Hutten, Guaiac could be used as a cure for the pains of the disease. As contact with the Americas
expanded, the record of American herbs and remedies grew. In 1570, King Phillip II appointed Francisco Hernandez as
chief physician of New Spain. However, the large-scale importation of exotic drugs from the New World did not take
root until the last decade of the 16th century.
Music
From this changing society emerged a common, unifying musical language, in particular the polyphonic style of the
Franco-Flemish school. The development of <color=#3366CC>printing</color> made distribution of music possible on a wide scale. Demand for
music as entertainment and as an activity for educated amateurs increased with the emergence of a bourgeois class.
Dissemination of <color=#3366CC>chansons</color>, motets, and <color=#3366CC>masses</color> throughout Europe coincided with the unification of polyphonic
practice into the fluid style that culminated in the second half of the sixteenth century in the work of composers such as
<color=#3366CC>Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina</color>, <color=#3366CC>Orlande de Lassus</color>, <color=#3366CC>Tomás Luis de Victoria</color>, and <color=#3366CC>William Byrd</color>.
Self-awareness
By the 15th century, writers, artists, and architects in Italy were well aware of the transformations that were taking place
and were using phrases such as modi antichi (in the antique manner) or alle romana et alla antica (in the manner of the
Romans and the ancients) to describe their work. In the 1330s <color=#3366CC>Petrarch</color> referred to pre-Christian times as antiqua
(ancient) and to the Christian period as nova (new). From Petrarch's Italian perspective, this new period (which
included his own time) was an age of national eclipse. Leonardo Bruni was the first to use tripartite <color=#3366CC>periodization</color> in his
History of the Florentine People (1442). Bruni's first two periods were based on those of Petrarch, but he added a third
period because he believed that Italy was no longer in a state of decline. Flavio Biondo used a similar framework in
Decades of History from the Deterioration of the Roman Empire (1439–1453).
Humanist historians argued that contemporary scholarship restored direct links to the classical period, thus bypassing
the Medieval period, which they then named for the first time the "Middle Ages". The term first appears in Latin in 1469
as media tempestas (middle times). The term rinascita (rebirth) first appeared, however, in its broad sense in <color=#3366CC>Giorgio</color>
<color=#3366CC>Vasari</color>'s <color=#3366CC>Lives of the Artists</color>, 1550, revised 1568. Vasari divides the age into three phases: the first phase contains

<color=#3366CC>Cimabue</color>, <color=#3366CC>Giotto</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Arnolfo di Cambio</color>; the second phase contains <color=#3366CC>Masaccio</color>, <color=#3366CC>Brunelleschi</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Donatello</color>; the third
centers on <color=#3366CC>Leonardo da Vinci</color> and culminates with <color=#3366CC>Michelangelo</color>. It was not just the growing awareness of classical
antiquity that drove this development, according to Vasari, but also the growing desire to study and imitate nature.
Spread
In the 15th century, the Renaissance spread rapidly from its birthplace in Florence to the rest of Italy and soon to the
rest of Europe. The invention of the <color=#3366CC>printing press</color> by German printer <color=#3366CC>Johannes Gutenberg</color> allowed the rapid
transmission of these new ideas. As it spread, its ideas diversified and changed, being adapted to local culture. In the
20th century, scholars began to break the Renaissance into regional and national movements.
England
The <color=#3366CC>Elizabethan era</color> in the second half of the 16th century is usually regarded as the height of the English
Renaissance. Many scholars see its beginnings in the early 16th century during the reign of <color=#3366CC>Henry VIII</color>.
The English Renaissance is different from the <color=#3366CC>Italian Renaissance</color> in several ways. The dominant art forms of the
English Renaissance were <color=#3366CC>literature</color> and <color=#3366CC>music</color>, which had a rich flowering. <color=#3366CC>Visual arts</color> in the English Renaissance
were much less significant than in the Italian Renaissance. The English Renaissance period in art began far later than
the Italian, which had moved into <color=#3366CC>Mannerism</color> by the 1530s.
In literature the later part of the 16th century saw the flowering of Elizabethan literature, with poetry heavily influenced
by <color=#3366CC>Italian Renaissance literature</color> but Elizabethan theatre a distinctive native style. Writers include <color=#3366CC>William Shakespeare</color>
(1564–1616), <color=#3366CC>Christopher Marlowe</color> (1564–1593), <color=#3366CC>Edmund Spenser</color> (1552–1599), Sir <color=#3366CC>Thomas More</color> (1478–1535), and
Sir <color=#3366CC>Philip Sidney</color> (1554–1586). English Renaissance music competed with that in Europe with composers such as
<color=#3366CC>Thomas Tallis</color> (1505–1585), John Taverner (1490–1545), and <color=#3366CC>William Byrd</color> (1540–1623). Elizabethan architecture
produced the large prodigy houses of courtiers, and in the next century <color=#3366CC>Inigo Jones</color> (1573–1652), who introduced
<color=#3366CC>Palladian architecture</color> to England.
Elsewhere, Sir <color=#3366CC>Francis Bacon</color> (1561–1626) was the pioneer of modern scientific thought, and is commonly regarded as
one of the founders of the <color=#3366CC>Scientific Revolution</color>.
France
The word "Renaissance" is borrowed from the French language, where it means "re-birth". It was first used in the
eighteenth century and was later popularized by French <color=#3366CC>historian</color> <color=#3366CC>Jules Michelet</color> (1798–1874) in his 1855 work, Histoire
de France (History of France).
In 1495 the <color=#3366CC>Italian Renaissance</color> arrived in France, imported by King <color=#3366CC>Charles VIII</color> after his invasion of Italy. A factor that
promoted the spread of secularism was the inability of the Church to offer assistance against the <color=#3366CC>Black Death</color>. <color=#3366CC>Francis I</color>
imported Italian art and artists, including <color=#3366CC>Leonardo da Vinci</color>, Primaticcio, Rosso Fiorentino, Niccolò dell'Abbate and
<color=#3366CC>Benvenuto Cellini</color> and built ornate palaces at great expense, like the <color=#3366CC>Palace of Fontainebleau</color> and the castle of
Chambord. Writers such as <color=#3366CC>François Rabelais</color>, <color=#3366CC>Pierre de Ronsard</color>, <color=#3366CC>Joachim du Bellay</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Michel de Montaigne</color>,
painters such as Jean Clouet and François Clouet, and musicians such as Jean Mouton also borrowed from the spirit
of the Renaissance. French Renaissance sculptors include Michel Colombe, Jean Goujon, Pierre Bontemps, Ligier
Richier and Germain Pilon while important architects of the time were Pierre Lescot, who built the Henri II aisle of the
Louvre, Philibert Delorme and Jacques I Androuet du Cerceau.
In 1533, a fourteen-year-old <color=#3366CC>Catherine de' Medici</color> (1519–1589), born in Florence to Lorenzo de' Medici, Duke of Urbino
and Madeleine de La Tour d'Auvergne, married <color=#3366CC>Henry II of France</color>, second son of King Francis I and Queen Claude.
Though she became famous and infamous for her role in the <color=#3366CC>French Wars of Religion</color>, she made a direct contribution in
bringing arts, sciences, and music (including the origins of <color=#3366CC>ballet</color>) to the French court from her native Florence.
Germany
In the second half of the 15th century, the Renaissance spirit spread to <color=#3366CC>Germany</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Low Countries</color>, where the
development of the printing press (ca. 1450) and Renaissance artists such as <color=#3366CC>Albrecht Dürer</color> (1471–1528) predated the
influence from Italy. In the early Protestant areas of the country humanism became closely linked to the turmoil of the
Reformation, and the art and writing of the German Renaissance frequently reflected this dispute. However, the <color=#3366CC>Gothic</color>
<color=#3366CC>style</color> and medieval scholastic philosophy remained exclusively until the turn of the 16th century. Emperor <color=#3366CC>Maximilian I</color>
of <color=#3366CC>Habsburg</color> (ruling 1493–1519) was the first truly Renaissance monarch of the <color=#3366CC>Holy Roman Empire</color>.
Hungary
After Italy, <color=#3366CC>Hungary</color> was the first European country where the Renaissance appeared. The Renaissance style came
directly from Italy during the Quattrocento (1400s) to Hungary first in the Central European region, thanks to the
development of early Hungarian-Italian relationships — not only in dynastic connections, but also in cultural, humanistic
and commercial relations – growing in strength from the 14th century. The relationship between Hungarian and Italian
Gothic styles was a second reason – exaggerated breakthrough of walls is avoided, preferring clean and light
structures. Large-scale building schemes provided ample and long term work for the artists, for example, the building of
the Friss (New) <color=#3366CC>Castle in Buda</color>, the castles of Visegrád, Tata, and Várpalota. In <color=#3366CC>Sigismund</color>'s court there were patrons
such as Pippo Spano, a descendant of the Scolari family of Florence, who invited Manetto Ammanatini and Masolino
da Panicale to Hungary.
The new Italian trend combined with existing national traditions to create a particular local Renaissance art. Acceptance
of Renaissance art was furthered by the continuous arrival of humanist thought in the country. Many young Hungarians
studying at Italian universities came closer to the <color=#3366CC>Florentine</color> humanist center, so a direct connection with Florence
evolved. The growing number of Italian traders moving to Hungary, specially to Buda, helped this process. New
thoughts were carried by the humanist prelates, among them Vitéz János, archbishop of Esztergom, one of the
founders of Hungarian humanism. During the long reign of Emperor Sigismund of Luxemburg the Royal Castle of Buda
became probably the largest <color=#3366CC>Gothic</color> palace of the late <color=#3366CC>Middle Ages</color>. King <color=#3366CC>Matthias Corvinus</color> (r. 1458–1490) rebuilt the
palace in early Renaissance style and further expanded it.
After the marriage in 1476 of King Matthias to Beatrice of Naples, Buda became one of the most important artistic
centers of the Renaissance north of the <color=#3366CC>Alps</color>. The most important humanists living in Matthias' court were Antonio
Bonfini and the famous Hungarian poet Janus Pannonius. András Hess set up a printing press in Buda in 1472.
Matthias Corvinus's library, the Bibliotheca Corviniana, was Europe's greatest collections of secular books: historical
chronicles, philosophic and scientific works in the 15th century. His library was second only in size to the <color=#3366CC>Vatican</color>
<color=#3366CC>Library</color>. (However, the Vatican Library mainly contained Bibles and religious materials.) In 1489, Bartolomeo della
Fonte of Florence wrote that Lorenzo de' Medici founded his own Greek-Latin library encouraged by the example of the
Hungarian king. Corvinus's library is part of UNESCO World Heritage.
Matthias started at least two major building projects. The works in Buda and Visegrád began in about 1479. Two new
wings and a hanging garden were built at the royal castle of Buda, and the palace at Visegrád was rebuilt in
Renaissance style. Matthias appointed the Italian Chimenti Camicia and the Dalmatian Giovanni Dalmata to direct
these projects. Matthias commissioned the leading Italian artists of his age to embellish his palaces: for instance, the
sculptor Benedetto da Majano and the painters Filippino Lippi and <color=#3366CC>Andrea Mantegna</color> worked for him. A copy of
Mantegna's portrait of Matthias survived. Matthias also hired the Italian military engineer Aristotele Fioravanti to direct
the rebuilding of the forts along the southern frontier. He had new monasteries built in <color=#3366CC>Late Gothic</color> style for the
<color=#3366CC>Franciscans</color> in Kolozsvár, <color=#3366CC>Szeged</color> and Hunyad, and for the Paulines in Fejéregyháza. In the spring of 1485, <color=#3366CC>Leonardo</color>
<color=#3366CC>da Vinci</color> travelled to Hungary on behalf of Sforza to meet King Matthias Corvinus, and was commissioned by him to
paint a <color=#3366CC>Madonna</color>.
Matthias enjoyed the company of Humanists and had lively discussions on various topics with them. The fame of his
magnanimity encouraged many scholars—mostly Italian—to settle in Buda. Antonio Bonfini, Pietro Ranzano,
Bartolomeo Fonzio, and Francesco Bandini spent many years in Matthias's court. This circle of educated men
introduced the ideas of <color=#3366CC>Neoplatonism</color> to Hungary. Like all intellectuals of his age, Matthias was convinced that the
movements and combinations of the stars and planets exercised influence on individuals' life and on the history of
nations. Martius Galeotti described him as "king and astrologer", and Antonio Bonfini said Matthias "never did anything
without consulting the stars". Upon his request, the famous astronomers of the age, Johannes Regiomontanus and
Marcin Bylica, set up an observatory in Buda and installed it with <color=#3366CC>astrolabes</color> and celestial globes. Regiomontanus
dedicated his book on navigation that was used by <color=#3366CC>Christopher Columbus</color> to Matthias.
Other important figures of Hungarian Renaissance include Bálint Balassi (poet), Sebestyén Tinódi Lantos (poet), Bálint
Bakfark (composer and lutenist), and Master MS (fresco painter).
Low Countries
Culture in the Netherlands at the end of the 15th century was influenced by the Italian Renaissance through trade via
<color=#3366CC>Bruges</color>, which made Flanders wealthy. Its nobles commissioned artists who became known across Europe. In science,
the <color=#3366CC>anatomist</color> <color=#3366CC>Andreas Vesalius</color> led the way; in <color=#3366CC>cartography</color>, <color=#3366CC>Gerardus Mercator</color>'s map assisted explorers and
navigators. In art, Dutch and Flemish Renaissance painting ranged from the strange work of <color=#3366CC>Hieronymus Bosch</color> to the
everyday life depictions of <color=#3366CC>Pieter Brueghel the Elder</color>.
Erasmus was arguably the Netherlands' best known humanist and Catholic intellectual during the Renaissance.
Northern Europe
The Renaissance in Northern Europe has been termed the "Northern Renaissance". While Renaissance ideas were
moving north from Italy, there was a simultaneous southward spread of some areas of innovation, particularly in <color=#3366CC>music</color>.
The music of the 15th-century Burgundian School defined the beginning of the Renaissance in music, and the
polyphony of the Netherlanders, as it moved with the musicians themselves into Italy, formed the core of the first true
international style in <color=#3366CC>music</color> since the standardization of <color=#3366CC>Gregorian Chant</color> in the 9th century. The culmination of the
Netherlandish school was in the music of the Italian composer <color=#3366CC>Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina</color>. At the end of the 16th
century Italy again became a center of musical innovation, with the development of the polychoral style of the Venetian
School, which spread northward into Germany around 1600. In <color=#3366CC>Denmark</color>, the Renaissance sparked the translation of
the works of Saxo Grammaticus into <color=#3366CC>Danish</color> as well as Frederick II and <color=#3366CC>Christian IV</color> ordering the redecoration or
construction of several important works of architecture, i.e. Kronborg, Rosenborg and Børsen.
The paintings of the Italian Renaissance differed from those of the Northern Renaissance. Italian Renaissance artists
were among the first to paint secular scenes, breaking away from the purely religious art of medieval painters. Northern
Renaissance artists initially remained focused on religious subjects, such as the contemporary religious upheaval
portrayed by <color=#3366CC>Albrecht Dürer</color>. Later, the works of <color=#3366CC>Pieter Bruegel the Elder</color> influenced artists to paint scenes of daily life
rather than religious or classical themes. It was also during the Northern Renaissance that <color=#3366CC>Flemish</color> brothers Hubert and
<color=#3366CC>Jan van Eyck</color> perfected the <color=#3366CC>oil painting</color> technique, which enabled artists to produce strong colors on a hard surface that
could survive for centuries. A feature of the Northern Renaissance was its use of the vernacular in place of Latin or
Greek, which allowed greater freedom of expression. This movement had started in Italy with the decisive influence of
<color=#3366CC>Dante Alighieri</color> on the development of vernacular languages; in fact the focus on writing in Italian has neglected a major
source of Florentine ideas expressed in Latin. The spread of the printing press technology boosted the Renaissance in
Northern Europe as elsewhere, with Venice becoming a world center of printing.
Poland
The Polish Renaissance lasted from the late 15th to the late 16th century and was the Golden Age of <color=#3366CC>Polish culture</color>.
Ruled by the <color=#3366CC>Jagiellonian dynasty</color>, the Kingdom of Poland (from 1569 known as the <color=#3366CC>Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth</color>)
actively participated in the broad European Renaissance. An early Italian humanist who came to Poland in the mid-15th
century was Filippo Buonaccorsi, who was employed as royal advisor and councillor. The tomb of John I Albert,
completed in 1505 by Francesco Fiorentino, is the first example of a Renaissance composition in the country. Many
Italian artists subsequently came to Poland with Bona Sforza of <color=#3366CC>Milan</color>, when she married King <color=#3366CC>Sigismund I</color> in 1518.
This was supported by temporarily strengthened monarchies in both areas, as well as by newly established
universities.
The Renaissance was a period when the multi-national Polish state experienced a substantial period of cultural growth
thanks in part to a century without major wars, aside from conflicts in the sparsely populated <color=#3366CC>eastern and southern</color>
<color=#3366CC>borderlands</color>. Architecture became more refined and decorative. Mannerism played an important part in shaping what is
now considered to be the truly Polish architectural style – high attics above the cornice with pinnacles and pilasters. It
was also the time when the first major works of <color=#3366CC>Polish literature</color> were published, particularly those of Mikołaj Rey and
Jan Kochanowski, and the <color=#3366CC>Polish language</color> became the <color=#3366CC>lingua franca</color> of East-Central Europe. The <color=#3366CC>Jagiellonian</color>
<color=#3366CC>University</color> transformed into a major institution of higher education for the region and hosted many notable scholars,
chiefly <color=#3366CC>Nicolaus Copernicus</color> and Conrad Celtes. Three more academies were founded at Königsberg (1544), Vilnius
(1579), and Zamość (1594). The Reformation spread peacefully throughout the country, giving rise to the <color=#3366CC>Nontrinitarian</color>
Polish Brethren. Living conditions improved, cities grew, and exports of agricultural products enriched the population,
especially the nobility (szlachta) and magnates. The nobles gained dominance in the new political system of Golden
Liberty, a counterweight to <color=#3366CC>monarchical</color> absolutism.
Portugal
Although Italian Renaissance had a modest impact in Portuguese arts, <color=#3366CC>Portugal</color> was influential in broadening the
European worldview, stimulating humanist inquiry. Renaissance arrived through the influence of wealthy Italian and
Flemish merchants who invested in the profitable commerce overseas. As the pioneer headquarters of European
exploration, <color=#3366CC>Lisbon</color> flourished in the late 15th century, attracting experts who made several breakthroughs in
mathematics, astronomy and naval technology, including Pedro Nunes, João de Castro, Abraham Zacuto, and <color=#3366CC>Martin</color>
<color=#3366CC>Behaim</color>. Cartographers Pedro Reinel, Lopo Homem, Estêvão Gomes, and Diogo Ribeiro made crucial advances in
mapping the world. Apothecary Tomé Pires and physicians Garcia de Orta and Cristóvão da Costa collected and
published works on plants and medicines, soon translated by Flemish pioneer botanist <color=#3366CC>Carolus Clusius</color>.
In architecture, the huge profits of the <color=#3366CC>spice trade</color> financed a sumptuous composite style in the first decades of the 16th
century, the Manueline, incorporating maritime elements. The primary painters were Nuno Gonçalves, Gregório Lopes,
and Vasco Fernandes. In music, Pedro de Escobar and Duarte Lobo produced four songbooks, including the
Cancioneiro de Elvas.
In literature, <color=#3366CC>Luís de Camões</color> inscribed the Portuguese feats overseas in the epic poem <color=#3366CC>Os Lusíadas</color>. Sá de Miranda
introduced Italian forms of verse and Bernardim Ribeiro developed pastoral romance, while plays by Gil Vicente fused it
with popular culture, reporting the changing times. <color=#3366CC>Travel literature</color> especially flourished: João de Barros, Fernão Lopes
de Castanheda, António Galvão, Gaspar Correia, Duarte Barbosa, and <color=#3366CC>Fernão Mendes Pinto</color>, among others, described
new lands and were translated and spread with the new printing press. After joining the Portuguese exploration of
Brazil in 1500, <color=#3366CC>Amerigo Vespucci</color> coined the term <color=#3366CC>New World</color>, in his letters to Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco de' Medici.
The intense international exchange produced several cosmopolitan humanist scholars, including Francisco de Holanda,
André de Resende, and Damião de Góis, a friend of Erasmus who wrote with rare independence on the reign of King
<color=#3366CC>Manuel I</color>. Diogo de Gouveia and André de Gouveia made relevant teaching reforms via France. Foreign news and
products in the Portuguese factory in <color=#3366CC>Antwerp</color> attracted the interest of <color=#3366CC>Thomas More</color> and <color=#3366CC>Albrecht Dürer</color> to the wider
world. There, profits and know-how helped nurture the Dutch Renaissance and <color=#3366CC>Golden Age</color>, especially after the arrival
of the wealthy cultured Jewish community expelled from Portugal.
Spain
The Renaissance arrived in the Iberian peninsula through the Mediterranean possessions of the <color=#3366CC>Crown of Aragon</color> and
the city of <color=#3366CC>Valencia</color>. Many early Spanish Renaissance writers come from the Crown of Aragon, including Ausiàs March
and Joanot Martorell. In the Crown of Castile, the early Renaissance was heavily influenced by the Italian humanism,
starting with writers and poets such as Íñigo López de Mendoza, marqués de Santillana, who introduced the new Italian
poetry to Spain in the early 15th century. Other writers, such as Jorge Manrique, Fernando de Rojas, Juan del Encina,
Juan Boscán Almogáver, and Garcilaso de la Vega, kept a close resemblance to the Italian canon. <color=#3366CC>Miguel de</color>
<color=#3366CC>Cervantes</color>'s <color=#3366CC>masterpiece</color> <color=#3366CC>Don Quixote</color> is credited as the first Western novel. Renaissance humanism flourished in the
early 16th century, with influential writers such as philosopher Juan Luis Vives, grammarian <color=#3366CC>Antonio de Nebrija</color> and
natural historian Pedro de Mexía. The poet and philosopher Luisa de Medrano, celebrated among her Renaissance
contemporaries as one of the puellae doctae ("learned girls"), was the first female professor in Europe at the <color=#3366CC>University</color>
<color=#3366CC>of Salamanca</color>.
Later Spanish Renaissance tended toward religious themes and mysticism, with poets such as Luis de León, <color=#3366CC>Teresa of</color>
<color=#3366CC>Ávila</color>, and <color=#3366CC>John of the Cross</color>, and treated issues related to the exploration of the <color=#3366CC>New World</color>, with chroniclers and
writers such as <color=#3366CC>Inca Garcilaso de la Vega</color> and <color=#3366CC>Bartolomé de las Casas</color>, giving rise to a body of work, now known as
Spanish Renaissance literature. The late Renaissance in Spain produced political and religious authors such as Tomás
Fernández de Medrano and artists such as <color=#3366CC>El Greco</color> and composers such as <color=#3366CC>Tomás Luis de Victoria</color> and Antonio de
Cabezón.
